exact_wording: We examined whether, within the same person, a day with more recorded Xbox/Nintendo play than that person's usual was associated with a different mood (affective valence, 0-100) at the next survey.
source_cell_or_key: Plan section 1; observed outcome min and max

exact_wording: Per additional hour of recorded linked-console play above a person's own usual, later mood differed by 0.07 points (95% interval -0.14 to 0.29) on the 0-100 scale. The interval lies entirely within +/-0.5 points per hour, the smallest effect we pre-set as meaningful, so associations larger than that are not supported in this cohort.

This conclusion was unchanged across the prespecified alternative analyses: nine alternative model fits (interval limits of 30, 36 and 72 hours and no limit; log-transformed and capped exposure; participants with at least five intervals; excluding zero-valued mood scores; a model with a random slope) and a classification using only the cluster-robust interval. For the log-exposure version, the comparison threshold is an approximate conversion.

exact_wording: Comparing intervals with any recorded play to none was imprecise: the estimate was 0.74 points (95% interval -0.68 to 2.15), so differences from about 0.68 points lower to about 2.15 points higher are compatible with the data.

exact_wording: These findings concern recorded play on linked Xbox/Nintendo accounts only, not gaming overall; intervals with no recorded session are not proof of no gaming.
With this sample we could reliably detect (80% power) associations of about 0.35 points per hour or larger, under the simulation's best-case assumptions of independent, normally distributed errors.
This is observational data: associations do not show that gaming changes mood, and a small association is not ruled out.

exact_wording: We analyzed 5,076 survey-to-survey intervals from 371 of the 419 participants with linked console accounts; the median interval was 24.43 hours (middle half: 23.27 to 27.03 hours).

Many model fits were singular (little person-to-person baseline variation after accounting for prior mood), and mood scores bunch near the top of the scale; we used robust standard errors and report the wider interval.
